reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone / Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
clinicalPearls: One of the commonest incidental bone lesions in children and adolescents, usually found by chance on radiographs taken for another reason
Typically located eccentrically in the metaphysis of long bones, especially around the knee and distal tibia
Radiographs show a well-defined, lobulated, eccentric lucency with a sclerotic scalloped margin and cortical thinning
Small cortical-based lesions are termed fibrous cortical defects, while larger medullary lesions are called non-ossifying fibromas; they are histologically identical
Most are asymptomatic and regress or ossify spontaneously with skeletal maturity, so no treatment is needed
Large lesions occupying a substantial portion of the bone width may carry a pathological fracture risk and warrant follow-up or fixation
Multiple lesions with cafe-au-lait macules and other features raise the possibility of Jaffe-Campanacci syndrome
reference.pathophysiology: Non-ossifying fibroma is a benign fibrous developmental lesion rather than a true neoplasm, arising in the metaphysis of growing bone. It is composed of spindle-shaped fibroblastic cells arranged in a storiform pattern, admixed with osteoclast-type giant cells and foamy lipid-laden macrophages. The lesion represents a localised failure of normal ossification at the metaphysis and characteristically migrates towards the diaphysis and involutes as the skeleton matures, often filling in with reactive bone. The eccentric cortical location and thin sclerotic rim reflect its slow, non-aggressive growth.
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiography, usually sufficient to make a confident diagnosis based on classic appearance
MRI or CT reserved for atypical features or to assess fracture risk in large lesions
Assessment of lesion size relative to bone width to estimate fracture risk
Clinical review for cafe-au-lait macules if multiple lesions are present
Biopsy only when imaging features are atypical or aggressive
redFlags: Large lesion occupying more than half the bone diameter with fracture risk
Aggressive or ill-defined margins atypical for a benign fibrous lesion
Persistent pain in the absence of fracture, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
Multiple lesions with extraskeletal features suggesting a syndrome
reference.prognosis: Non-ossifying fibroma is benign and self-limiting, with the overwhelming majority resolving spontaneously by early adulthood and requiring no intervention. Outcomes are excellent, and treatment is reserved for the uncommon large lesion at fracture risk.
pitfalls: Performing unnecessary biopsy of a classic incidental lesion that could be diagnosed radiographically
Overlooking fracture risk in a large lesion of a weight-bearing bone
Failing to recognise multiple lesions as a possible syndromic association
Confusing it with more aggressive fibro-osseous lesions on limited imaging
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours
Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
management: Observe the typical asymptomatic lesion without intervention, as no treatment is needed for this benign self-limiting entity
Rely on plain radiography for diagnosis and avoid biopsy when the appearances are classic
Follow up with interval radiographs to document spontaneous regression and ossification with skeletal maturity
Estimate pathological fracture risk from lesion size relative to bone width, using CT or MRI for large lesions
Treat large lesions at fracture risk, or those that have fractured, with curettage, bone grafting and internal fixation
Advise protected weight-bearing and activity modification while a substantial lesion remains at risk
Assess for café-au-lait macules and syndromic associations when multiple lesions are present
